newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Italy budget to avoid new taxes, welfare cuts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Italy budget to avoid new taxes, welfare cuts.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi got the go-ahead on Wednesday to introduce a corrective mini-budget which will weigh on business but steer clear of tax hikes or cuts to welfare spending, coalition allies said.

The package, needed to keep Italy on track for joining European economic and monetary union (EMU), will include around 16 trillion lire ($9.5 billion) of deficit-cutting measures and is expected to be approved by the cabinet on Thursday.
Leaders from the centre-left coalition parties agreed the broad outline of the budget at a meeting with Prodi.
"There are all the conditions necessary for the cabinet to introduce the budget tomorrow," said Massimo D'Alema, leader of the large Democratic Party of the Left (PDS).

Full details of the package were not revealed, but the head of the hardleft Communist Refoundation party, Fausto Bertinotti, told reporters he had won his battle to prevent any tax hikes or cuts to social spending.
"This is undoubtedly a socially balanced budget with all the requests put forward by the right and by (the employers) thrown out," Bertinotti said.
Around two thirds of the deficit-saving measures will come from cuts to unspecified state funds and a re-organisation of the tax system, the hardleft leader said.

The rest will come by obliging firms to stump up taxes on huge severance payment funds two years ahead of time and by holding back end-of-contract retirement settlements to state workers for six months.

Firms regularly dip into the severance savings, held over for employees when they retire, as a cheap source of self-financing and have warned that any raids on these resources would harm trade at a weak moment in the business cycle.

Statistics office Istat said on Wednesday that the unemployment rate rose to 12.4 percent of the work force in January from 12.2 percent last October, while employers' body Confindustria said industrial output fell 2.9 percent year-on-year in March.

But the government had little alternative to tapping into the severance funds given that Refoundation, which holds the balance of power in the lower house of parliament, had vetoed any immediate cuts to the welfare state.

Opposition centre-right parties had called on Prodi to make structural cuts to social spending, arguing that this was the only way to ensure that Italy was ready for the launch of the single European currency, scheduled for January 1999.

Initial data from the first quarter of 1997 indicated that unless corrective measures were introduced, Italy's deficit this year was heading towards 3.8 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) against three percent demanded by the Maastricht Treaty.
Former finance minister Giulio Tremonti, a member of Silvio Berlusconi's Forza Italia party, blasted the budget, saying the advance tax on severance funds would create unemployment.
"For the rest, it is just a collection of accounting inventions and falsifications, which is typical of a dead political body," he said.

Analysts also bemoaned the lack of structural changes in the budget package. "Not only are these one-off measures, these are one-off measures that will come back with a vengeance next year...they are trying to sweep the problem under the carpet," said Giovanni Mossetti, chief economist at Milan brokers Caboto.
But the government pledged to launch a review of the welfare state as soon as the budget was introduced.
"It seems there is wide agreement on the need for this," said cabinet secretary Enrico Micheli. "The method and the timeframe for this will be decided shortly."
